summary: Comments on the file transfer proposal in RFC 114. The author thinks it is not strict enough about transactions: every message should get a reply and control should pass back and forth until the server ends the session. It also discusses error recovery during transfers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 133 comments on the file-transfer proposal in RFC 114. It suggests acknowledging each transaction, adding ways to access records and list files, and recovering from errors in stages.

subtitle: Suggestions for handshaking, file access, and error recovery in an early transfer protocol.

tldr.problem: The file-transfer proposal in RFC 114 needed clearer transaction acknowledgments and more detailed error recovery.
tldr.mechanism: R. L. Sunberg proposes a reply for every transaction, record access and directory listing requests, multilevel recovery, and NCP version inquiries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 133 updates RFC 114 with suggestions; it does not define a finished protocol.

today: RFC 133 updates RFC 114 with comments and proposals. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: A Reply for Each Transaction
sections.content:
Sunberg argues that each transaction should prompt a response from its recipient. Control should pass back and forth until the server ends the exchange, so the server always has the last word.

The RFC gives sample retrieve and store exchanges. In a retrieve, the user asks for a file, receives acknowledgment that the server has it, requests the data, and acknowledges the returned parts before the server reports completion.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal has the sender and receiver acknowledge each step. The server ends the exchange with the final response.

sections.title: Record Access and File Listings
sections.content:
The proposal adds a key to store and retrieve requests so they can access an individual record in a file. A retrieve with a key returns the record after the matching key; a store replaces that record or appends one if the key is not present.

A lookup request can list key names in a file. A new transaction code F requests a file-directory listing for one or more pathnames.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of transferring an entire file, a request can identify a record by key. Another request can list files that match given pathnames.

sections.title: Recovering from Errors in Stages
sections.content:
If an error preserves transaction boundaries and affects only one side of a duplex connection, the parties can abort the current transaction sequence and try again. The example includes retrying after a data error or a timeout.

If that recovery fails, the proposal clears and resynchronizes the link. It suggests adding an 8-bit argument to the NCP interrupt-on-link messages INR and INS. Closing the faulty socket is the last resort.
sections.plainLanguage: The first response to an error is to stop the current exchange and retry. If the link cannot be resynchronized, the parties can close the socket.

sections.title: NCP Version Inquiry
sections.content:
Sunberg suggests adding a version number to the Network Control Program (NCP). The next version would include WRU, which asks the receiving host for its version, and IAM, which supplies it.

The author suggests that the version field be 32 bits to leave room for expansion. At first, the exchange could indicate whether the hosts can communicate; later, it might indicate what each host can do.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts could ask which NCP version the other host has. The author suggests a large field so it could later describe capabilities too.
